title: Information Technology Act, 2000 — Section 66A (Struck Down — Not Operative)

content.overview: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 formerly penalised sending by means of a computer resource or communication device any information that was grossly offensive or had menacing character, or was known to be false and caused annoyance, inconvenience, danger, obstruction, insult, injury, criminal intimidation, enmity, hatred or ill will, among other formulations. Section 66A was struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court and is not operative law. Do not charge, advise or examine under s. 66A as current law. Other IT Act provisions or general criminal law may apply only if their own ingredients are independently satisfied.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Is the proposed charge under s. 66A? → Stop. (2) Do other operative IT Act or BNS ingredients fit the facts instead?
content.study:
Exam answers must state that s. 66A is not good law. Shreya Singhal is the constitutional invalidation reference for verification — not expanded as invented holding text here.

No new case invented.

sections.heading: Former text (historical)
sections.body: s. 66A formerly targeted grossly offensive or menacing information and certain false information causing annoyance and related harms sent by computer resource — as then enacted.

sections.heading: Current status
sections.body: s. 66A is not operative following constitutional invalidation. It must not be treated as current criminal law.

sections.heading: Exam and advisory rule
sections.body: Refuse s. 66A as a live charge; map facts to other operative provisions only if their ingredients are met.

sections.heading: Alternative paths
sections.body: Depending on facts: other IT Act offences (e.g. ss. 66C, 66D, 67), defamation, criminal intimidation or other BNS offences — each on its own terms.

sections.heading: Method
sections.body: If s. 66A is suggested, state it is struck down; then test alternative operative sections fact-by-fact.

provisions.title: Punishment for sending offensive messages (struck down — not operative)

examples.title: Offensive social media post
examples.body: A complaint invokes only s. 66A for an offensive post — advise that s. 66A is not operative; evaluate other statutes solely on their ingredients.

hypotheticals.question: Can police still register an FIR under s. 66A?
hypotheticals.analysis: s. 66A is not operative law after constitutional invalidation; reliance on it as a live offence is legally unsound.

distinctions.title: s. 66A (dead) vs operative IT Act offences
distinctions.right: ss. 66, 66C–66F, 67 etc. remain available on their own ingredients.

misconceptions.trap: s. 66A can still be used for online insults.
misconceptions.correction: s. 66A is constitutionally invalid and must not be treated as current law.
